review:
Your $10 rerelease of a cartoonishly difficult 30-year-old game has no save states or other quality of life features, I am pirating your game so that I do not have to waste upwards of 15 minutes replaying levels I've already beaten just to have another attempt at beating one I haven't.

I [i]love[/i] Umihara Kawase: the insane level design and precision platforming; the near-infinite ceiling for skill expression; the mostly tough-but-fair difficulty; the calming music and laidback atmosphere; and the quirky artwork. 

There's a lot I [i]hate[/i] about it, too: the unhinged amounts of RNG enemy spam in late-game levels; the all-or-nothing arcade-style gameplay (i.e. no continues when you exhaust your lives); the occasionally janky-feeling hit/hurt boxes and collision effects; and the often tedious boss fights. At its worst, it not only feels dated (it [i]was[/i] released in 1994 after all) but downright busted.

That this game won me over after repeatedly crushing my resolve is a testament to how fun and fresh it still feels. Yes, even despite the flaws (sorry, the random enemy spawning just plain sucks). If you have copious patience and enjoy a game opening up as you gain skill, this could become one of your new favorite titles. That said, I haven't been this stressed out 100%-ing a game since I beat the Pantheon of Hallownest in Hollow Knight years ago. Seriously: if you can't cope with the idea of watching 20+ minutes of progress go down the toilet, steer clear.

But Umihara Kawase is one of the best, most infuriating and ultimately fun games I've ever played.

If you like challenging old school platformers this is the game for you. Umihara Kawase is a game that will get your heart pumping as difficult trials and tribulations are thrown your way. You must pull off tricky stunts and daring maneuvers through the sky using your fishing rod as you deal with enemy spawns that constantly keep you on your toes; the excitement that this game provides is unparalleled by other titles.

One thing that really makes this game stand apart from its peers is just how high the skill ceiling is. It is unbelievable seeing speedruns of this game and realizing just how quickly you can soar through levels. With the games built-in online leaderboards you are able to see just how fast players destroy each level. A level that may take a new player 3 minutes to complete can often times be beaten in 10 seconds by elite players of the game. Both on a casual and advanced scope, this game pushes players towards satisfying levels of mastery as you learn tech that allows you to make the most out of the games wild physics. Sporting 49 unique levels with 60 exits, the game has a lot of levels that allow players to really hone their skills. Replaying levels feels like a reward as you come face to face with a level that once challenged you and you are able to find new paths through the level, saving you lots of time while testing your skills.

Regarding the negatives of this game, by far the biggest sin that this game commits are its boss battles. One or two of them can be a bit fun but there are some very long boss battles that can be summed up as survival challenges where you are tasked with surviving a difficult situation for several minutes. While these can be cool the first time you come across them, they get old rather quickly and can become quite tedious as you play through the game. This game also lacks a few QOL features that one might expect in the modern era of gaming, although there are mods online that can help alleviate some of those issues.

Overall if you like difficult platformers I can't recommend this title enough. This game often goes on sale for around $2, and its one of the best purchases you can make on Steam. This game has become my second favourite game of all time, only behind its sequel Umihara Kawase Shun which can also be found on Steam in a similar price range.

Below is not actually a review, but a short game manual, because the game tells you precisely nothing, and you don't get the real manual that was probably bundled along with the SNES physical release.

BASIC CONTROLS:
Up to shorten your line, down to lengthen it. In particular, since you'll most frequently be dangling down from a ceiling, you'll usually go up by pressing down and down by pressing up.
You can grab and climb up ledges by pressing left or right. Not up. You don't need to press up to climb.
Shoulder buttons to peek left and right.

ADVANCED TECHNIQUES:
Here are four techniques that are pretty much necessary to beat the game.
1.Rocket jumping: a technique to greatly enhance your horizontal jumping ability. Hook yourself to the ground at your feet. Don't modify the line's length and run as far as your line allows in the direction opposite of your destination. Keep running and make a short jump. Switch the direction of your movement in midair. As you pass in front of your hook, release it. Jump again as soon as your feet touch the ground. The point is to use the extra speed provided by the tugging of your fishing line while keeping ground friction to a minimum.
2.Overcoming bottom corners: you're dangling down from a platform's bottom edge, you want to climb on top of it, or at least reattach yourself a bit higher on the platform's left or right edge, here's how to do it. Lengthen the line enough to give you some horizontal swinging space. Swing a bit to accumulate speed. When you're at about the extreme opposite of where you want to go (so if you're trying to go up the right edge of a platform the right moment would be about when you're swinging as much to the left as possible) press down. The speed from your swinging and from your line shortening will add up, and if you release the hook at the right timing, you'll be going up in whatever direction you wanted. If you release earlier you can also use this to give yourself horizontal speed instead.
3.Wall climbing: barely a technique and more of a reminder. You can climb high vertical walls. Just attach yourself to it and swing up and down, if you time your swinging and your hook release correctly, you'll go up, it's that easy.
4.Extreme horizontal jump: a variation of (2.) useful here and there because it's easier than acquiring speed through swinging. You're standing on a sufficiently large platform, there's a pretty high ceiling above you and you want to jump very far (like a whole screen away) in the distance. Hook yourself up, keep the line length as is. Run towards to opposite direction. You'll notice that Kawase's feet are actually a bit sticky, allowing you to tug at the rope, but there's a limit to it, if you keep running you'll detach yourself from the ground. As you run, right before the line forces you away from the ground, jump (you're still going in the wrong direction at that point). Then, at the apex of your jump, start pressing down on your controller. Release yourself at the right timing and you'll be flying a whole screen away.

TIMER BOSS FIGHTS:
It's important to know that a few bosses in the game, especially the first you're likely to run into, don't take any kind of damage from your actions. They're timer bosses, you beat them by surviving for a while and there's nothing you can do to shorten the time needed to beat them.

STANDARD ENEMIES:
You can kill a stunned enemy by having it hooked near yourself. Some enemies can be killed in the same way without being stunned, and some enemies need to be stunned to be killed but can only be stunned by pulling them strongly enough to detach them from the ground, which is usually done by attaching yourself to them before falling down.

30 AND 5 MINUTE RULE:
There are four "endings" to the game, with four final levels that lead you to them. If a run goes on for more than 30mn and you go through a door, that door will automatically bring you to one of those four final levels, skipping the rest of the game altogether. One of those final levels in particular is only reachable this way.
There is a cheat code that changes those 30mn into just 5. You just need to press select precisely 100 times on the menu.

100% COMPLETION RULES:
You're free to challenge yourself any way you want, but here are the actual rules to both the steam and ingame achievements.
A level or an ending is considered reached and available in training mode either if you actually played the level in the normal mode, or if you managed to go through a door that would have brought you to that level. So if you go through a door but the 30mn rule teleports you to a final level, the game will still consider that you reached the level that was supposed to be behind the door.
Bags are considered picked up even if you do it in training, same goes for beating enemies.
A door is considered cleared even if you only reached it in training, the game does remember and show that you did it that way though.

MONSTER SPAWN AND FLYING CLAMS:
I do not know precisely how the monster spawning mechanics of the game work, but I do know one thing which is that in at least some levels, the spawn is influenced by the monsters you killed. In particular, some levels punish you for killing enemies by spawning in flying clams, which are probably the strongest enemies in the game.

I bought this back in 2019 as soon as I saw the SNES aesthetic (completely unaware this originally released in 1994) but soon dropped it because I couldn't make much progress past the tadpole.
I got back into it this year, and I'm happy I did so. Few games give off the same feeling that this one does. It's whimsical, innocent and unassuming, but oozing with charm.
This version only contains the original versions of the songs (not the remixes from the DS version), but these sound better anyway. Shoutouts to whoever on the development team decided to swap the Mountain Stream (Keiryuu) and Waterfall (Taki) themes, as they fit their new areas much better than in the original version (especially for Field 42).
Fields 36 and 45 can rarely crash the game. I don't know how to reproduce the Field 36 crash, but for Field 45 just don't grab the top of the fallen bridge and you'll be fine. The pace of the gameplay thankfully means you don't lose much (if any) progress, as you're constantly replaying the stages and honing your skills until you can finally beat that dang crab!
The game contains a "forgiveness mechanic" in that it will dump you into one of the ending levels once your current run reaches 30 minutes. You can change this timer to 5 minutes by pressing whatever the Select button is mapped to 100 times on the title screen (and there's an achievement for this too, for some reason). A practice mode is included in this release too!

I really enjoy this game! It takes a little practice to use the fishing rod properly, but once you get the hang of it, it's extremely satisfying. I can't quite place a good comparison most people would know-- I'm only drawing the ninja rope from Worms Armageddon, but there's more spring here. The "precision platformer" tag for this game mostly comes from mastering this physics-based mechanic.  

Be warned: it's a hard game. It'll take practice to see an ending (from achievements, only about 5% of players have beaten the game, and less than 20% have gotten past the first boss, which serves as the first real skill check). If you go in with the right mindset and understand this is more of a run-based hi-score arcade game than a typical A to B platformer, you'll have a good time.

Fun fact: Bennet Foddy cited this series as inspiration for streamer-bait sensation Getting Over It. Tbh, I think he mostly meant the random 3D asset visuals from the third game (Sayonara Umihara Kawase), but I could see the game design being an inspiration too. Definitely had my fair share of fumbling a swing or being knocked back by an enemy, winding up down at the start of the level. Luckily the levels are short and the mechanics are sweet, so it's not nearly as punishing. 

Having put some time into the entire series, I think this is the one to go for. Subjectively, it feels the most responsive and I enjoy the physics the most (it feels well-tuned and weighty vs. feeling a little more slippery and exaggerated to me in the later games), though granted this is also the one I started with. They're all solid really, so if you prefer the aesthetics of a later game, give that one a go!

Edit: I've come to believe Shun's better. The level design's got a bit more going on and the physics have grown on me.

Umihara Kawase最初於1994年12月出現在Super Famicom上，但直到2015年才獲得正式的英文版本，當時它被作為獎金遊戲與Sayonara的PS Vita版本（現在是PC版本的獨立版本）一起收錄。

這個遊戲的目標是從一個階段的開始，通過你可靠的魚竿到達一扇門（有時你可以選擇兩扇門，更難到達的一扇門是通往後面田地的捷徑），我的意思是你必須抓住， 在躲避敵人（有腿的魚和一兩個老闆）的同時，在古怪的平臺關卡上搖擺和跳躍，並使用你瘋狂的橡皮筋物理技能快速到達出口（如果你想快速奔跑或給朋友留下深刻印象）。 遊戲要麼在你耗盡生命，要麼到達最後一扇出口門時結束。

在某些關卡之前，遊戲會向你展示一件你可以做的事情來度過這個關卡，無論是如何跨越一些差距，還是如何應對敵人，或者只是幫助你在遊戲中獲勝的東西。

我不建議在鍵盤上玩這個，因為它支持控制器，而且與使用控制器/手持系統玩該系列中的任何遊戲相比，感覺都要好得多。 但如果你能掌握鍵盤控制，那麼你就是一個很酷的人。

音樂很好，很簡單，但我想很吸引人。

這場比賽剛開始的時候，有一件事是能够保存重播。 這個功能仍然存在，但你也有排行榜，所以如果你喜歡排行榜上的東西，那麼你就可以去了。

對大多數人來說，學習很容易，對一些人來說，掌握一輩子。 我是川澤友原。

一気にクリアするゲームだと考えると海腹川背さんは少し難しすぎるかもしれません。
１日にちょっとの時間、ミニゲーム感覚で遊ぶと健全に楽しむ事ができると思います。

このゲームはスキルの上達を感じ始めると途端に面白くなってきますよ。

Really amazing platformer with a very specific charm you can't find anywhere else thanks to the graphics, music, art direction, and fish. Controls are fun and unique, very stylistically appealing imo. It's an old snes game so with that comes obnoxious difficulty, pretty much once you get a game over you have to start the entire game over again. There's no way to save, extra lives are very scarce, and reaching a new level will likely result in you getting a game over due to trial and error. It kind of feels like doing runs in a roguelike. Once you complete a stage you're able to access it from the main menu to do a practice run, this will not do anything other than letting you practice that one stage that you already completed. It sounds a little useless but it's actually really helpful because once you get it down you can get through it with all you're lives next time you do a "run" and then save them for the next new level.

伸縮自在のゴムを操作してステージを縦横無尽に飛び回るラバーリングアクションゲーム。
元々はSFCでリリースされた作品でPC移植版が本作となる。

最初に注意点としてXbox360コントローラーは非推奨だ。
繊細な十字キー操作が要求されるので、誤爆しやすいコントローラーはNGとなる。
（それでも筆者は360コンしかないので、それでプレイし続けた）

ゲーム自体はラバーの挙動が独特で操作性は非常に難しい。
思ったよりも物理の挙動がしっかりされているので慣れるのに時間を要するだろう。

慣れれば数々のテクニックを駆使して難所もショートカットで快適に進めるようになったりと、一度クリアしたステージでも時間を掛けずに進めるようになるので、自身の上達を実感しやすいのも魅力的だ。

アクションが苦手でも引っかけたルアーを離さなければ落下死することはほぼ無いステージ構成が殆どなので、焦らずに丁寧なプレイングを心がけることで攻略自体は可能だろう。

SFC版準拠の移植作品だが、練習モードが実装されているので任意のステージをクリア出来るまで試行錯誤しやすくなっている。

本作にはコンテニューがなく、ステージセレクトもなかったりとアーケードライクな作りになっている。
心折設計に感じる部分だが、練習モードで集中的に練習しやすく、エンディング自体も1周30分程で見られる設計なので、一番簡単な攻略ルートならそこまで欠点という程でもない。

本作で不満な要素を上げるならボス戦がある。
特に大型ボスは倒すことが出来ないので一定時間生存すると扉が開放される遅延コンテンツなのですこぶる評判が悪い。

【総評】
諦めずに練習し続ければ上達を実感しやすいレベルデザインが秀逸で、エンディングに到達したときの達成感が過去一で得られるアクションゲームが本作だ。

振り子操作が苦手な筆者でも全実績達成できたので皆も諦めずに頑張って欲しい。
ちなみに筆者の初エンディング到達のプレイ時間は12時間程。

人によっては壺おじと比較する人も居るだろうが、不用意にルアーを離さなければ落下することのない本作と比べるなら雲泥の差だと思う。

Great game with wonderfully executed mechanics and a few design problems. The mechanics are explored to the maximum potential over the course of the game and the levels have branching paths which allow the player to take different (longer or shorter) routes to the finish line.

The main problems arise with the "bosses" and the enemy spawn rates. The bosses bring the pace of the game to a halt because they consist mostly of waiting out phases until the boss gets too bored or kills itself. Normal enemies will spawn randomly in the normal levels and this can lead to cheap deaths while platforming. 

Overall, though, it's a fun and rewarding game for those willing to put in the effort and practice.

Crée par un studio japonais indé et publié par NHK (la chaine publique japonaise) en 1994.

Je préfère les mario-like, ici, on ne peut pas sauter sur les ennemies, il faut les capturer, pourtant je m'amuse dans cette plage de sérénité.
Le panel de mouvement est limité, mais grâce au fil de pêche et à son hameçon, vous pouvez vous parer à toutes situations, il sert aussi de grappin.
Je vais tenter de réussir les succès, cela ajoute un challenge pour ce genre jeu.

C'est une bonne touche nostalgique qui va vous faire revenir en enfance.
